summary: All three Basic Sole Trader runs read as credible accounts for the trades described: bricklayer with sub-contract labour and materials above gross profit, IT consultancy with a small stock/direct element and heavy overheads, and a taxi driver whose largest expense is motor costs. Nothing blocking; a few presentational and classification points are noted below for a human to glance at, none of which stop the run.

concerns.figure: Income Tax P&L line C30 = 0 while "Tax at basic rate" C32 carries the whole charge (£1,792 / £105,395 / £3,808.40)
concerns.where: Profit & Loss Account, cells C30 and C32, all three runs
concerns.why: The line labelled Income Tax shows nil in every run and the tax actually sits on the row below. Self-consistent and the totals chain through to Net Income After Tax, but a reader looking at the P&L would think no income tax had been computed. Worth confirming the label/cell mapping is intended.

concerns.figure: Tax at basic rate £105,395 with Tax at Higher Rate £97,854.80 on taxable income £282,338
concerns.where: bst-scenario-basic, Profit & Loss C32 and Income Tax E8/E9
concerns.why: The P&L row labelled "Tax at basic rate" carries the full income tax including the higher-rate element, and the sheet has no additional-rate (45%) band or personal-allowance taper at £294,908 profit. The arithmetic is internally consistent with the injected two-band Admin rates, so this is a product scope point rather than a mis-post, but the resulting liability understates a real 2027 return.

concerns.figure: New Asset Cost (Plant & Machinery) £1,800 against Total Original Cost £39,000
concerns.where: bst-scenario-basic, Fixed Assets E67 vs E1
concerns.why: The reported single-asset figure is only the first of three additions; the schedule total is correct at £39,000. Presentational only, but a reader comparing the two lines will query the £37,200 gap.

concerns.where: bst-scenario-basic, Profit & Loss C17 and C18 (journal codes a and l)
concerns.why: Two unrelated expense codes carrying an identical annual total is unusual for 393 real purchase entries and suggests the source data reuses one amount. Not material to profit, worth a look at the source journal.

concerns.figure: Cost of Sales £10,540 and Direct Costs £8,000 in an IT consultancy
concerns.where: bst-scenario-basic, Profit & Loss C6 and C7, plus Stock opening £10,000 / closing £6,000
concerns.why: A software and consultancy business holding £6,000–£10,000 of stock is atypical; the amounts are small relative to £409,900 turnover and are consistent with the declared journal codes s and d, so this does not distort the accounts, but the stock element deserves a sanity check against what is actually held.

concerns.figure: Other Expenses £17,882 (code o) as the second largest overhead
concerns.why: An unanalysed "other" line of £17,882, larger than premises, admin, legal and motor individually, is the kind of catch-all a reviewer would want broken down before the accounts are filed. It is fed by a declared journal code so it is not missing money.

concerns.figure: Fixed asset addition £200 taken as AIA for a private hire driver, with no vehicle on the schedule
concerns.where: bst-sp-sixty, Fixed Assets E1 and Purchase Analysis £200
concerns.why: A taxi business with £38,000 of fares shows only a £200 capital addition and no car on the fixed asset schedule, so no vehicle depreciation or WDA arises. Consistent with the scenario (motor costs claimed as actual running costs, £2,708) and the Admin motor restriction is unused, but the absence of the trade's main asset is worth noting.

concerns.figure: All debtor and creditor slots shown as dashes; Stock opening, at cost and closing all £0
concerns.where: bst-sp-sixty, Debtors & Creditors and Stock sections
concerns.why: Every working capital line is empty. The scenario declares no debtor, creditor or stock entries and a cash-basis taxi driver holding no stock is plausible, so these zeros are the product working as designed rather than lost data.
